method: Numbers were read on 2026-11-14 from the abstract or full text (publisher page, Europe PMC full text, or the official PDF) by a research sub-agent and spot-checked. The url field is the DOI or publisher landing page for the reader. verified=false rows were NOT confirmed at source and must never be used as model inputs; they are kept only so the gap is visible.

rows.unit: strategy indicator
rows.claim: National Cancer Strategy 2026-2035, objective 3 'Ensuring equal and effective cancer care': five-year survival of poor-prognosis cancers reaches the Nordic level (lung +14 pp, pancreas +6 pp, liver +14 pp vs the 2023 NORDCAN level; Nordic = mean of Sweden and Norway); cancer mortality decreases by 10% (currently 13,300 deaths per year); patients access treatment within the established target times (THL Ohjaus 21/2016).
rows.citation: Ministry of Social Affairs and Health / FICAN. National Cancer Strategy 2026-2035. Figure 1 and section 3.

rows.unit: % participation target in every wellbeing services county
rows.claim: All cancer screening programmes achieve an 80% participation rate in each wellbeing services county; at least 70% of cancers are diagnosed at stages I to II.
rows.citation: National Cancer Strategy 2026-2035, Figure 1.

rows.unit: finding
rows.claim: Currently no unified national system guides disease-specific care guidelines or the implementation and monitoring of care pathways; existing guidelines, pathways, targets and indicators are not coordinated nationally, which perpetuates regional inequalities in access to and effectiveness of cancer care.
rows.citation: National Cancer Strategy 2026-2035, sub-objective 3.1.

rows.unit: EUR billion in 2035 (1.5 in 2023)
rows.claim: Cancer care costs are projected to rise from about EUR 1.5 billion (2023) to EUR 2.6 billion (2035) without targeted measures.
rows.citation: Kansallinen syöpästrategia 2026-2035, pp. 7-8.

rows.unit: days (mean symptom-to-treatment, public primary care minus private/occupational: 207 vs 123)
rows.claim: Finnish DLBCL cohort (n=160): mean cumulative days from symptom onset via private/occupational vs public primary care: first contact 42 vs 72, physician visit 43 vs 94, referral 77 vs 147, specialist visit 118 vs 204, treatment start 123 vs 207.
rows.citation: Kuitunen J, et al. Socioeconomic Status and Access to Treatment in Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma. Cancer Med 2026;15(5):e71920, Figure 1 (values read from the figure).
rows.notes: Single cancer type, 39 private/occupational vs 48 public primary-care-appointment patients, observational. The milestone means are read from Figure 1, not from the text; the text gives means 201 vs 126 days (a 75-day difference) and medians 127 vs 76 (51 days). Used as a labelled transferable prior for the shape of the route gap, not as a measured value for other cancers. First author Joonas Kuitunen (re-checked 2026-11-14 23:00 UTC in the utupub PDF, sha256 34c8e9b9dc0162642e45de3cce8f28e84ec89ffb4965a11ff6300dcb7cd739a2).

rows.unit: days (median symptom-to-treatment, 127 public vs 76 private/occupational; p=0.027)
rows.claim: Median symptom-to-treatment interval was 127 days for patients whose first contact was a public primary-care appointment (48 patients; mean 201) and 76 days via private or occupational care (39 patients; mean 126); Mann-Whitney U p = 0.027.
rows.citation: Kuitunen J, et al. Socioeconomic Status and Access to Treatment in Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma. Cancer Med 2026;15(5):e71920, p. 4 (results text) and Table 1 (contact place).

checked.how: utupub PDF opened and read with pdftotext; Europe PMC full text returned HTTP 503 at 22:53 UTC

rows.notes: One cohort of one cancer (diffuse large B-cell lymphoma); 87 patients in the two route groups; observational.

rows.unit: percentage points 2-year PFS (89% vs 74%, p=0.012)
rows.claim: In Finnish DLBCL, a symptom-to-biopsy interval over 7 weeks was associated with lower 2-year progression-free survival (74% vs 89%).
rows.citation: Tokola S, et al. Cancer Med 2025;14(22):e71409.
rows.notes: Observational; no hazard ratio in the abstract.

rows.unit: hazard ratio of death per 4-week delay
rows.claim: Each 4-week delay of breast cancer surgery is associated with HR 1.08 for death.
rows.citation: Hanna TP, et al. Mortality due to cancer treatment delay: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ 2020;371:m4087.

rows.unit: hazard ratio of death per 4-week delay
rows.claim: Each 4-week delay of colectomy is associated with HR 1.06 for death.
rows.citation: Hanna TP, et al. BMJ 2020;371:m4087.

rows.unit: hazard ratio of death per 4-week delay
rows.claim: Each 4-week delay of lung cancer surgery is associated with HR 1.06 for death; the interval includes 1.
rows.citation: Hanna TP, et al. BMJ 2020;371:m4087.
rows.notes: Not statistically significant; propagate the full interval.

rows.unit: hazard ratio of death per 4-week delay
rows.claim: Each 4-week delay of adjuvant systemic therapy for colorectal cancer is associated with HR 1.13 for death.
rows.citation: Hanna TP, et al. BMJ 2020;371:m4087.

rows.unit: hazard ratio of death per 4-week delay
rows.claim: Each 4-week delay of adjuvant systemic therapy for breast cancer is associated with HR 1.09 for death.
rows.citation: Hanna TP, et al. BMJ 2020;371:m4087.

rows.unit: days, median diagnostic interval after vs before
rows.claim: After Denmark introduced standardised cancer patient pathways, the median diagnostic interval was 17 days shorter in 2010 than in 2004/05; patients not referred to a pathway waited 4 days longer.
rows.citation: Jensen H, Tørring ML, Olesen F, Overgaard J, Fenger-Grøn M, Vedsted P. Diagnostic intervals before and after implementation of cancer patient pathways. BMC Cancer 2015;15:308.
rows.notes: Before/after without control group; two-tier risk for patients outside the pathway.

rows.unit: 1-year excess hazard ratio, pathway-referred vs not
rows.claim: Danish patients referred through a cancer patient pathway had a 1-year excess hazard ratio of 0.86 (0.73-1.01) vs patients not referred; 3-year relative survival rose from 45% to 54% across the implementation period.
rows.citation: Jensen H, Tørring ML, Vedsted P. Prognostic consequences of implementing cancer patient pathways in Denmark. BMC Cancer 2017;17:627.
rows.notes: Interval includes 1; lead-time and secular-trend bias acknowledged by authors.

rows.unit: relative participation, self-sampling kit vs reminder letter
rows.claim: In a Finnish randomised trial among cervical screening non-attenders, a mailed HPV self-sampling kit gave relative participation 1.21 vs a reminder letter.
rows.citation: Virtanen A, et al. Self-sample HPV tests as an intervention for nonattendees of cervical cancer screening in Finland: a randomized trial. Cancer Epidemiol Biomarkers Prev 2011;20(9):1960-1969.

rows.unit: percentage points (72.6% to 79.2% with reminder letters, 82.2% adding self-sampling)
rows.claim: In Finland, reminder letters raised cervical screening participation from 72.6% to 79.2% and adding self-sampling raised it to 82.2%.
rows.citation: Virtanen A, et al. Improving cervical cancer screening attendance in Finland. Int J Cancer 2015;136(6):E677-E684.

rows.unit: relative participation, mailed kit vs letter (pooled RCTs)
rows.claim: Mailing HPV self-sampling kits to under-screened women gave pooled relative participation 2.33 vs invitation or reminder letters.
rows.citation: Arbyn M, et al. Detecting cervical precancer and reaching underscreened women by using HPV testing on self samples: updated meta-analyses. BMJ 2018;363:k4823.
rows.notes: International pooled estimate; the Finnish trial effect is much smaller and is the one used in the model.

rows.unit: rate ratio, 10-year lung-cancer mortality (men)
rows.claim: In the NELSON trial, volume CT screening of current and former heavy smokers reduced 10-year lung-cancer mortality in men (rate ratio 0.76).
rows.citation: de Koning HJ, et al. Reduced lung-cancer mortality with volume CT screening in a randomized trial. N Engl J Med 2020;382:503-513.
rows.notes: Applies to the screened high-risk group only, not to all lung cancer deaths.

rows.unit: % reduction in screen-reading workload; detection ratio 1.29 (1.09-1.51)
rows.claim: In the MASAI randomised trial, AI-supported mammography reading reduced radiologist screen-reading workload by 44% with a cancer detection ratio of 1.29.
rows.citation: MASAI trial investigators. Screening performance and characteristics of breast cancer detected in the MASAI trial. Lancet Digit Health 2025;7(3):e175-e183.
rows.notes: Interval-cancer result was non-inferior, not superior: supports capacity relief, not a survival claim.

rows.unit: hazard ratio of diagnostic resolution, navigated vs usual care (days 91-365)
rows.claim: Patient navigation increased the rate of diagnostic resolution after 90 days (adjusted HR 1.51) and of treatment start (HR 1.43).
rows.citation: Freund KM, et al. Impact of patient navigation on timely cancer care: the Patient Navigation Research Program. J Natl Cancer Inst 2014;106(6):dju115.
rows.notes: US safety-net populations; effect seen for patients already delayed beyond 90 days.

rows.unit: odds ratio of stage IV at diagnosis, lower vs higher education (women; men 1.10, 1.08-1.12)
rows.claim: In 469,522 Finnish cancer patients (2000-2019), lower education was associated with higher odds of stage IV disease at diagnosis.
rows.citation: Zai X, Li P, Dei Bardi L, et al. Disparities in cancer incidence, stage at diagnosis, treatment and mortality across socioeconomic groups in Finland. BMJ Public Health 2025;3(2):e002829.

rows.unit: hazard ratio of death, lower vs higher education (women; men 1.13, 1.10-1.16)
rows.claim: Lower education was associated with higher mortality after a cancer diagnosis in Finland.
rows.citation: Zai X, et al. BMJ Public Health 2025;3(2):e002829.

rows.unit: systematic review, 98 studies, no pooled estimate
rows.claim: Across 98 Nordic studies, lower socioeconomic status was associated with more advanced stage, less active treatment and poorer survival.
rows.citation: Ammitzbøll G, et al. Socioeconomic inequality in cancer in the Nordic countries. A systematic review. Acta Oncol 2022;61(11):1317-1331.

rows.unit: Atkinson inequality-aversion parameter (median, general public, England)
rows.claim: Elicited public inequality aversion implies health gains to the least healthy fifth are weighted several times those to the healthiest fifth.
rows.citation: Robson M, Asaria M, Cookson R, Tsuchiya A, Ali S. Eliciting the level of health inequality aversion in England. Health Econ 2017;26(10):1328-1334.

rows.unit: methods reference
rows.claim: Distributional cost-effectiveness analysis quantifies who gains and who loses from a health policy and the trade-off between total health and health inequality.
rows.citation: Cookson R, et al. Using cost-effectiveness analysis to address health equity concerns. Value Health 2017;20(2):206-212.

rows.unit: not used
rows.claim: Multi-cancer early detection blood tests: the first randomised trial (NHS-Galleri) reportedly missed its primary endpoint; no mortality evidence. Not included as an intervention.
rows.citation: NHS-Galleri, ASCO 2026 (secondary report only).
rows.notes: Kept to document why MCED is excluded.

rows.unit: not retrieved
rows.claim: The numeric national target times for access to cancer treatment (THL Ohjaus 21/2016) could not be read at source in this session. The product therefore lets the user set the target-time threshold and does not assert a legal value.
rows.citation: THL. Hoitoonpääsyn seuranta syövän hoidossa. Ohjaus 21/2016.
rows.notes: Open gap: confirm with AstraZeneca mentors or THL.

rows.unit: percentage points of five-year relative survival, higher minus lower education (men 77 vs 64, women 78 vs 65)
rows.claim: The Finnish Cancer Registry found five-year survival estimates of 64% (men) and 65% (women) among people with lower education levels, significantly lower than 77% and 78% among people with higher education levels. Regional estimates do not significantly differ.
rows.quote: Estimates do not significantly differ across regions
rows.citation: OECD/European Commission. EU Country Cancer Profile: Finland 2025. p. 20.

checked.how: official PDF opened and read with pdftotext

rows.notes: Individual-level registry figures reported by the OECD/EU; the profile gives no years for the education split. All cancers.

rows.unit: percentage points, breast screening participation, higher minus lower education (85 vs 66), 2020-21
rows.claim: Age-standardised breast cancer screening participation was lower among women with lower (66%) than higher (85%) education levels (2020-21).
rows.citation: OECD/European Commission. EU Country Cancer Profile: Finland 2025. p. 15.

checked.how: official PDF opened and read with pdftotext

rows.unit: percentage points, breast screening participation, Finnish, Swedish or Sami speakers minus non-domestic language speakers (82 vs 63), 2020-21
rows.claim: Breast cancer screening participation was lower among non-domestic language speakers (63%) than among women speaking Finnish, Swedish and Sami (82%) (2020-21).
rows.citation: OECD/European Commission. EU Country Cancer Profile: Finland 2025. p. 15.

checked.how: official PDF opened and read with pdftotext

rows.unit: percentage points, cervical screening participation, higher minus lower education (78 vs 51)
rows.claim: A 2023 Finnish Cancer Registry review found cervical screening participation of 78% among women with higher education levels against 51% among women with lower education levels.
rows.citation: OECD/European Commission. EU Country Cancer Profile: Finland 2025. p. 15.

checked.how: official PDF opened and read with pdftotext

rows.unit: percentage points, cervical screening participation, domestic minus non-domestic language speakers (73 vs 57)
rows.claim: Cervical cancer screening participation differs between domestic language speakers (73%) and speakers of a non-domestic language as their mother tongue (57%).
rows.citation: OECD/European Commission. EU Country Cancer Profile: Finland 2025. p. 15.

checked.how: official PDF opened and read with pdftotext

rows.unit: % breast screening participation in Helsinki, 2017-21 (lowest; Åland highest at 86)
rows.claim: Between 2017 and 2021 the lowest age-standardised breast screening participation was in Uusimaa, particularly Helsinki (73%), likely because opportunistic screening outside the programme is more frequent in the capital city; Åland had the highest rate (86%).
rows.quote: This is likely because opportunistic screening outside the screening programme is more frequent in the capital city.
rows.citation: OECD/European Commission. EU Country Cancer Profile: Finland 2025. p. 15.

checked.how: official PDF opened and read with pdftotext

rows.unit: days (six weeks), reported maximum waiting-time target, suspected-cancer referral to start of primary treatment
rows.claim: The OECD/EU profile reports that Finland has maximum waiting time targets for access to specialised treatment, such as six weeks between a referral concerning a suspected case of cancer and the start of primary treatment.
rows.quote: such as six weeks between a referral concerning a suspected case of cancer and the start of primary treatment
rows.citation: OECD/European Commission. EU Country Cancer Profile: Finland 2025. p. 19.

checked.how: official PDF opened and read with pdftotext

rows.notes: Reported by the OECD/EU, not read in Finnish law. SAMA uses 42 days only as a labelled placeholder threshold.

rows.unit: months, statutory maximum from established need to start of non-urgent specialised care
rows.claim: Finland's statutory care guarantee for non-urgent specialised care: assessment of the need for care starts within three weeks of the referral arriving, the tests and specialist assessment within three months, and care within six months of the need being established. The page names no cancer-specific limit.
rows.quote: se on aloitettava viimeistään kuudessa kuukaudessa hoidon tarpeen toteamisesta
rows.citation: Ministry of Social Affairs and Health (STM). Hoitotakuu (treatment guarantee), updated 29 Oct 2026.

rows.unit: wellbeing services counties (plus the City of Helsinki, which organises its own services)
rows.claim: There are a total of 21 wellbeing services counties; the Region of Uusimaa is divided into four counties, and the City of Helsinki is responsible for organising health, social and rescue services within its area.
rows.quote: There are a total of 21 counties.
rows.citation: Ministry of Social Affairs and Health (STM). Wellbeing services counties (undated page).
rows.notes: SAMA's 23 areas are these 21 counties, the City of Helsinki and Åland (HVA91), which the page does not list.
